abstract: ATP8A2 is a P4-ATPase that actively flips phosphatidylserine and to a lesser extent phosphatidylethanolamine across cell membranes to generate and maintain transmembrane phospholipid asymmetry. The importance of this flippase is evident in the finding that loss-of-function mutations in ATP8A2 are known to cause the neurodevelopmental disease known as cerebellar ataxia, intellectual disability, and dysequilibrium syndrome 4 (CAMRQ4) in humans and related neurodegenerative disorders in mice. Although significant progress has been made in understanding mechanisms underlying phospholipid binding and transport across the membrane domain, little is known about the structural and functional properties of the cytosolic N- and C-terminal segments of this flippase. In addition, there has been uncertainty regarding the methionine start site of ATP8A2 and accordingly the size of the N-terminal segment. Here, we have used mass spectrometry to show that bovine ATP8A2 like its human counterpart has an extended N-terminal segment not apparent in the mouse ortholog. This segment greatly enhances the expression of ATP8A2 without affecting its cellular localization or phosphatidylserine-activated ATPase activity. Using a cleavable C-terminal protein and site-directed mutagenesis, we further show that the conserved GYAFS motif in the C-terminal segment plays a role in autoinhibition as well as efficient folding of ATP8A2 into a functional protein.
methods:
Experimental procedures
Reagents
1,2-Dioleoyl-
sn
-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC) and 1,2-dioleoyl-
sn
-glycero-3-phospho-L-serine (DOPS) were purchased from Avanti Polar Lipids, Inc. ATP and ascorbic acid were purchased from Sigma–Aldrich, CHAPS from Anatrace, ProteaseArrest inhibitor cocktail from G-Biosciences, and 1D4 peptide from Biomatik. HEK293T and HeLa cells were purchased from American Type Culture Collection through Cedarlane Laboratories. The Rho 1D4 antibody used in the immunoaffinity columns was initially generated in-house (
53
); the purified antibody was obtained from the University of British Columbia (
https://uilo.ubc.ca/industry-partners/access-ubc-technologies
). Primary antibodies against tubulin were ordered from Abcam (ab15568). Primary antibodies against ATP8A2 (ATP6C11) used in Western blots were raised in-house (
19
,
36
). Restriction enzymes, T4-DNA ligase, Antarctic Phosphatase, and Phusion polymerase were acquired from New England Biolabs. Primers used for mutagenesis were ordered from Integrated DNA Technologies. Purified TEV protease was received as a gift by Dr Van Petegem (UBC).
N- and C-terminal mutant construct design
The bovine and human ATP8A2 constructs containing a C-terminal 1D4 tag were previously developed in a pcDNA3.1 plasmid (
36
). The single amino acid substitutions in the GYAFS motif were generated by designing specific overlapping primers with mismatched nucleotides for PCR using Phusion polymerase. A construct containing a TEV protease cut site (ENLYFQ▼S) inserted at the −60 C-terminal amino acid position was created using overlapping primer design. Constructs were created in which the start codons of the human ATP8A2 construct were truncated to the 40th and 47th amino acid position. These constructs were then ligated back into the WT plasmid construct using the KpnI and EcoRI restriction enzymes. The bovine ATP8A2 N terminus was truncated at the 37th amino acid using PCR and ligated back into the original plasmid construct using the KpnI and BamHI restriction enzymes.
Cell culture and protein expression
HEK293T cells were cultured using DMEM (Sigma–Aldrich) supplemented with 8% bovine growth serum (Thermo Scientific), 100 IU/ml penicillin, 100 μg/ml streptomycin, and 2 mM
l
-glutamine. The cells were grown to ∼30% confluency in 10 cm plates at which point they were cotransfected with 5 μg of the ATP8A2 construct and 5 μg CDC50A plasmid and 30 μg of polyethylenimine as a transfection reagent. The cells were harvested after 48 h and pelleted at 2000 rcf (Sorvall LegendRT). The cells were resuspended in lysis buffer (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM Hepes/NaOH [pH 7.5], 5 mM MgCl
2
, 20 mM CHAPS, 1× Protease Arrest, 1 mM DTT, and 0.5 mg/ml DOPC). The resuspended cells were lysed by stirring at 4 °C for 30 min. After lysis, the detergent insoluble membrane fraction was removed from the detergent soluble fraction by centrifugation at 40,000 rcf for 12 min. The solubilized ATP8A2–CDC50A proteins were then used for downstream applications. Protein expression was measured using Western blot analysis and normalized to a tubulin loading control (see later).
Immunoaffinity protein purification
Purification of the ATP8A2–CDC50a complex was achieved using immunoaffinity column chromatography as previously described (
19
,
36
). Immunoaffinity columns were prepared through the coupling of the Rho1D4 or ATP6C11 monoclonal antibodies to CNBr-activated Sepharose 2B beads as described previously (
36
,
54
). Typically, the detergent-solubilized cell lysate was incubated with the immunoaffinity matrix for 45 min at 4 °C. The unbound protein was then removed by centrifugation, and the spin column containing the immunoaffinity matrix was then washed six times with 400 μl of column wash buffer (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM Hepes/NaOH pH 7.5, 5 mM MgCl
2
, 10 mM CHAPS, 1 mM DTT, and 0.5 mg/ml DOPC). The bound protein was eluted from the column using 2 × 50 μl of wash buffer containing 0.5 mg/ml of the 6C11 or 1D4 peptide. Purified protein concentration was determined from SDS-PAGE stained with Coomassie blue and quantified relative to bovine serum albumin as standards.
TEV cleavage of TEV-modified ATP8A2
The ATP8A2 construct containing a C-terminal TEV cut site was purified as described. After purification and quantification, the sample was incubated with TEV protease at a ∼1:1 w/w ratio at 4 °C overnight. Uncleaved ATP8A2 and C-terminal peptide fragments were removed by binding to an anti-6C11 immunoaffinity column. This was verified using Western blot analysis in combination with Coomassie-stained SDS gels.
ATPase assays
The ATPase activity of the purified ATP8A2 constructs was assayed using a previously described colorimetric method (
36
,
55
). To measure the ATPase activity as a function of lipid substrate, 1 ng of purified protein was incubated with 5 mM ATP and 2.5 mg/ml of different ratios of DOPC:DOPS. To measure the velocity as a function of ATP concentration, 1 ng of protein was incubated with 2.5 mg/ml of lipid mixture (68:32 DOPC:DOPS), and variable concentrations of ATP ranging from 0 mM to 5 mM. The ATP and lipid samples were prepared in ATPase assay buffer (50 mM Hepes/NaOH, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 12.5 mM MgCl
2
, 1 mM DTT, and 10 mM CHAPS). This mixture was prepared up to 25 μl and was incubated at 37 °C for 30 min. The activity of the protein was terminated through the addition of 25 μl of 12% SDS. The free phosphate was measured by the addition of 75 μl of solution 1 (6% ascorbic acid and 1% ammonium molybdate in 1 N HCl) for 5 min, followed by 120 μl of solution II (2% sodium citrate, 2% sodium meta-arsenite, and 2% acetic acid). The reaction of solution 1 and solution 2 results in a color shift allowing for the measurement of free phosphate absorbance at 850 nm in a microplate reader. These values were compared to those of a phosphate standard curve allowing for calculation of the reaction velocity (micromoles of Pi released/minute/milligram protein) for each data point in the given assay. Each measurement was performed in technical triplicates. Michaelis–Menten equation was used to fit the data and obtain maximum reaction velocity (
V
max
), PS-activation constant (
K
a
), and PS-activation constant (
K
a
) and
K
m
for ATP.
Immunofluorescence microscopy
HeLa cells grown on glass coverslips in six-well tissue culture plates were cotransfected at 50% confluence with 1.25 μg of ATP8A2-1D4 and 1.25 μg of CDC50A plasmids using polyethylenimine as a transfection agent. After 48 h, the cells were washed in PBS and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, then blocked and permeabilized for 1 h with 10% normal goat serum (Sigma–Aldrich, NS02L) and 0.2% Triton X-100. The cells were treated for 2 h with primary antibody diluted in 100 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) containing 2.5% normal goat serum and 0.05% Triton X-100. The primary antibodies were Rho1D4 hybridoma culture fluid (1:50 dilution), and rabbit anti-GM130 antibody (1:2000, SAB5700801; Sigma–Aldrich) for labeling the cis-Golgi. The coverslips were washed and labeled with goat antimouse immunoglobulin tagged with AlexaFluor 488 (A11029; Thermo Fisher Scientific) and goat antirabbit immunoglobulin tagged with AlexaFluor 594 (A11012; Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 0.5 h and stained with the nuclear dye 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole. Coverslips were washed and mounted with Mowiol medium (Sigma–Aldrich; 32459-0) on glass slides prior to imaging. The reagents for fixing, permeabilizing, and labeling were prepared in 100 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.4). The secondary antibodies were used at 1:1000 dilution. Fluorescence images were acquired using a 63× oil immersion objective on a Zeiss LSM 700 confocal microscope equipped with Zen Image analysis software (
https://www.zeiss.com/microscopy/en/products/software/zeiss-zen-lite.html
). Composite figures were prepared using Photoshop software. Quantification of colocalization was performed using Coloc2, a plugin of ImageJ (National Institutes of Health,
https://imagej.nih.gov/ij/
). The Pearson correlation coefficient was reported for the ATP8A2 and GM130 signals.
SDS-PAGE and Western blotting
Proteins were separated by SDS gel electrophoresis on 9% polyacrylamide gels and either stained with Coomassie blue or transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride membranes (Millipore) and blocked with 1% milk in PBS for 45 min as previously described (
44
). The blots were labeled with hybridoma cell culture fluid containing the Rho1D4 antibody (diluted 1:100 in PBS). The blots were also labeled with antitubulin antibody (1:3000 dilution) serving as a loading control. After 1 h, the gels were washed stringently with PBS containing 0.05% Tween-20 (PBST), incubated for 40 min with secondary antibody (goat antimouse conjugated with IR dye 680 or donkey antirabbit conjugated with IR dye 800; 926-68070 and 926-32213; LI-COR) diluted 1:20,000 in PBST containing 0.5% milk. After washing in PBST, the blots were imaged on a LI-COR Odyssey infrared imaging system (
https://www.licor.com/bio/image-studio-lite/
).
AlphaFold analysis and
in silico
stability predictions
The stability of WT and ATP8A2 clones was predicted using FoldX5 (
https://foldxsuite.crg.eu/
) (
50
) as previously described (
43
). The protein structures were generated in AlphaFold2 (
56
) and repaired using the FoldX5 plugin with the YASARA viewer (
http://www.yasara.org/
). The structure of ATP8A2 (accession number:
Q9NTI2
) was accessed from the AlphaFold database (
https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/
). This was accessed on July 10, 2023. The Gibbs free energy change was calculated and reported as ΔΔGmutant−ΔΔGWT. PyMOL Molecular Graphics System (version 1.7; Schrodinger) was used to display structures.
LC–MS/MS analysis
Protein samples for MS analysis were purified from bovine rod outer segments and HEK293T transfected cells using immunoaffinity protein purification. Rod outer segments were isolated from bovine retina as previously described (
57
) and solubilized in 20 mM CHAPS detergent. The cell lysate was incubated with Atp-6C11 antibody conjugated to Sepharose 4B. The beads were eluted using 50 μl of SDS elution buffer (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM Hepes/NaOH [pH 7.5], 5 mM MgCl
2
, 1% SDS, 1 mM DTT, and 0.5 mg/ml DOPC). Approximately 5 μg of purified protein sample was acquired for each condition. The samples were then subjected to proteolysis for MS using the filter-aided sample preparation as described previously (
15
,
58
).
Samples were reconstituted in 0.5% acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid. Sample concentration was measured using NanoDrop One (Thermo Scientific) with the A205 Scope method (absorbance at 205 nm, baseline correction at 340 nm). About 100 ng of peptides were injected and separated on-line using NanoElute 2 UHPLC system (Bruker Daltonics) with Aurora Series Gen3 (CSI) analytical column, (25 cm × 75 μm 1.7 μm C18 120 Å, with CSI fitting; Ion Opticks). The analytical column was heated to 50 °C using a column toaster M (Bruker Daltonics). The NanoElute thermostat temperature was set at 7 °C. Buffer A consisted of 0.1% aqueous formic acid and 0.5% acetonitrile in water, and buffer B consisted of 0.1% aqueous formic acid and 0.5% water in acetonitrile. Before each run, the analytical column was conditioned with four column volumes of buffer A. The analysis was performed at 0.30 μl/min flow rate. A standard 30 min gradient was run from 2% B to 12% B over 15 min, then to 33% B from 15 to 30 min, then to 95% B over 0.5 min, held at 95% B for 7.72 min. Liquid chromatography was coupled to a Trapped Ion Mobility-Time of Flight mass spectrometer with dual TIMS (TimsTOF Pro2; Bruker Daltonics). The captive spray ionization source was operated at 1800 V capillary voltage, 3 L/min drying gas, and 180 °C drying temperature. During analysis, the TimsTOF Pro 2 was operated with parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation scan mode for data-dependent acquisition. The MS and MS/MS spectra were collected in positive mode, from
m/z
100 Th to
m/z
1700 Th, and from ion mobility range (1/K0) 0.7 V∗s/cm
2
to 1.35 V∗s/cm
2
. A polygon filter was applied to the mass to charge and the ion mobility plane to include the most likely peptide precursors and to reduce singly charged background ions. TIMS-MS scan was set at equal ramp time and accumulation time of 100 ms, at a rate of 9.42 Hz (100% duty cycle). Active exclusion was enabled with a 0.4 min release and reconsidered if their intensity increased more than four times. For each TIMS cycle, five parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation MS/MS scans were recorded (total cycle time = 0.64 s). Target intensity for parent ions was set to 10,000 cts/s with a threshold of 1000 cts/s. Isolation widths were set at 2.07
m/z

m/z

2
to 55 eV at 1/k0 = 1.35 V s/cm
2
. TimsTOF Pro 2 was run with timsControl v. 5.0.4 (Bruker Daltonics). LC and MS were controlled with HyStar 6.2 (6.2.1.13; Bruker). The mass-to-charge ratio and ion mobility value were calibrated based on three selected ions from Agilent ESI-Low Tuning Mix ions (
m/z
[Th], 1/k0 [Th]: 622.0290, 0.9915; 922.0098, 1.1986; 1221.9906, 1.3934). The mass accuracy was typically within 4 ppm and is not allowed to exceed 7 ppm. All acquired data were searched on Byonic (PMI-Byonic-Com:v4.0.12; Protein Metrics) against
Homo sapiens
or
Bos taurus
database with trypsin cleavage sites (RK), and up to two missed cleavage sites were allowed. Peptide mass tolerance was set to 20 ppm, and fragment mass tolerance was 30 ppm. Cysteine carbamidomethylation (+57.021464) was set as a fixed modification; glutamine deamidation (+0.984016) and methionine oxidation (+15.994915) were set as variable modification. The false discovery rate was controlled to <1% at the protein level.
Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis of the data was carried out using GraphPad Prism 9.0 (
https://www.graphpad.com/
). Data were expressed as a mean ± SD for n independent experiments. Where applicable, unpaired two-tailed
t
test was used.
body:
P4-ATPases comprise a subfamily of P-type ATPases that actively transports lipids, notably phospholipids, across cell membranes (
1
,
2
,
3
,
4
,
5
). This generates and maintains transmembrane lipid asymmetry, which plays a central role in a variety of cellular processes, including membrane curvature, vesicle transport, phagocytosis, apoptosis, sperm maturation, blood coagulation, synaptic modeling, and cell migration among others (
6
,
7
,
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
). The importance of P4-ATPases is evident in the finding that genetic defects in many of these flippases are associated with monogenic and complex human diseases.
The human genome codes for 14 P4-ATPases (ATP8A1, ATP8A2, ATP8B1, ATP8B2, ATP8B3, ATP8B4, ATP9A, ATP9B, ATP10A, ATP10B, ATP10D, ATP11A, ATP11B, and ATP11C) based on their α-subunits and two accessory β-subunits referred to as CDC50A and CDC50B (also known as TMEM30A and TMEM30B) (
11
,
12
). The mouse genome contains a gene that encodes an additional P4-ATPase referred to as
ATP8B5
and a gene that encodes a third β-subunit known as
CDC50C
(
13
,
14
). In the human genome, however, these are considered as pseudogenes. Twelve human P4-ATPases form a heterodimer with CDC50A; three P4-ATPases (ATP8B1, ATP8B2, and ATP8B4) can also form a heterodimer with CDC50B; and two P4-ATPases (ATP9A and ATP9B) do not require a β-subunit (
15
,
16
,
17
,
18
). The various P4-ATPases differ in their lipid substrate specificity, tissue expression, and subcellular localization (
5
).
Like other P-type ATPases, the α-subunit of P4-ATPases is the principal catalytic subunit. It consists of a membrane domain consisting of 10 transmembrane helical segments that functions in the binding and translocation of lipid substrates across the membrane and three cytoplasmic domains, an N-domain involves in nucleotide binding, a P-domain that undergoes transient phosphorylation, and an A-domain that functions in dephosphorylation of the phosphorylated intermediate as part of the catalytic reaction cycle. The smaller β-subunit, consisting of two transmembrane segments that flank a relatively large glycosylated exoplasmic domain, plays a crucial role in the proper folding of the P4-ATPase into an active lipid flippase (
19
,
20
). Biochemical studies together with recent high-resolution X-ray and cryo-EM structures of P4-ATPases in various states have provided insight into the binding and translocation of lipids across membranes, subunit interactions, and conformational transitions that occur as part of the reaction cycle (
21
,
22
,
23
,
24
,
25
,
26
,
27
,
28
). The N- and C-terminal segments of several P4-ATPases have been characterized (
29
). In the case of ATP8B1 and yeast Drs2, these segments reduce the phospholipid-dependent ATPase activity of these flippases through an autoinhibition mechanism (
27
,
28
,
30
,
31
,
32
). The N- and C-terminal regions of other P4-ATPases including ATP8A1, and the ATP11, ATP10, and ATP9 subclasses, play a role in the targeting of these flippases to specific cell membranes (
29
,
33
,
34
).
ATP8A2 is a P4-ATPase that is primarily expressed in the cerebellum, testis, retina, and spinal cord (
35
,
36
,
37
). It associates with CDC50A to form a heterodimer that actively flips phosphatidylserine (PS) and to a lesser extent phosphatidylethanolamine from the exoplasmic to the cytoplasmic leaflet of biological membranes (
19
,
36
,
38
). As shown for both ATP8A1 and ATP8A2, the flipping of PS creates transmembrane lipid asymmetry, which facilitates the trafficking of receptors to the plasma membrane of cells (
39
). The importance of ATP8A2 in cell physiology is highlighted by the finding that loss-of-function mutations in ATP8A2 cause a severe neurodevelopmental disease known as cerebellar ataxia, intellectual disability, and dysequilibrium syndrome 4 (CAMRQ4) in humans and related neurodegenerative and sensory disorders in mice (
35
,
37
,
40
,
41
,
42
). Site-directed mutagenesis has been valuable in identifying key amino acid residues important for the binding and translocation of phospholipids across membranes (
21
,
22
,
38
). Analysis of disease-associated mutations has also identified specific residues in the cytoplasmic and transmembrane domains required for the proper folding and function of human ATP8A2 (
22
,
41
,
43
,
44
,
45
,
46
). In contrast, few studies have been directed toward defining the properties of the N-terminal and C-terminal regions of this flippase (
47
). In the present study, we show by mass spectrometry (MS) and biochemical studies that bovine and human ATP8A2, unlike mouse ATP8A2, have an extended N-terminal segment that strongly enhances protein expression without altering their functional properties. We also define the contribution of the C-terminal segment and specific residues within a highly conserved GYAFS motif on the expression and activity of ATP8A2.
Results
Analysis of the N terminus of bovine ATP8A2 by MS
The α-subunit of the ATP8A2–CDC50A complex from various vertebrates shares a high degree of sequence conservation within the canonical region of the protein (
Figs. 1
,
A
and
B
and
S1
). For example, human, bovine, and mouse ATP8A2 are over 93% identical in sequence downstream of the methionine that defines the beginning of the canonical region. This methionine that lies just upstream of the start of the A-domain is listed in the UniProt database (
https://www.uniprot.org
) as the initiation site for both mouse (
P98200
) and bovine (
C7EXK4
) ATP8A2. In contrast, the initiation site for human ATP8A2 (
Q9NTI2
) is considered to be 40 amino acids upstream of this methionine resulting in an extended N terminus. The sequence of exon 1 for the human, bovine, and mouse ATP8A2 genes is available. Translation of the mRNA transcript for exon 1 of human and bovine ATP8A2 shows several potential translation initiation sites (
Fig. S2
). At present, however, there are no experimental data to confirm the initiation site for ATP8A2 from any species, and therefore, the length and role of the N terminus of ATP8A2 remains unclear.

We have used LC–MS/MS to detect tryptic peptides of ATP8A2 from native tissue for comparison with well-defined ATP8A2 overexpressed in human embryonic kidney 293T (HEK293T) cells. We chose to analyze the bovine protein since bovine tissue is more readily available for ATP8A2 purification and analysis, and bovine ATP8A2 has been the subject of numerous biochemical studies (
21
,
36
,
48
).

Tables S1

). Over 159 unique peptides covering 48% of the protein were observed for ATP8A2, and 45 unique peptides covering over 33% of the protein were detected for CDC50A derived from bovine retina. Similar numbers of peptides were identified from the recombinant ATP8A2–CDC50A complex expressed and isolated from HEK293T cells.

As expected, peptide fragments upstream of the canonical ATP8A2 sequence were present for recombinant ATP8A2 expressed in HEK293T cells (
Fig. 1
D
). These peptides were also observed for ATP8A2 isolated from bovine retina. In addition, several peptides were observed that extended even further upstream of the expressed recombinant ATP8A2 (
Fig. 1
D
and
Table 1
). These studies indicate that the methionine 37 residues upstream of the canonical sequence is the primary initiation site for ATP8A2 in bovine retina and closely coincides with the predicted start site of human ATP8A2 (
Fig. 1
B
). It is possible that the other two methionine residues can serve as alternative start sites, but this remains to be determined.
Expression and functional characterization of human and bovine N-terminal-truncated ATP8A2 variants
To determine whether the N-terminal region of human ATP8A2 affects protein expression and/or function, human ATP8A2, constructs encoding proteins with the deletion of the N-terminal 40 (ATP8A2-NΔ40) and 47 (ATP8A2-NΔ47) amino acids were cloned into pcDNA3.1 for cotransfection with CDC50A in HEK293T cells (
Fig. 2
A
). The cell lysates were solubilized in CHAPS detergent and subsequently resolved on SDS-polyacrylamide gels for analysis of ATP8A2 expression levels by quantitative Western blotting. The human ATP8A2-NΔ40 and ATP8A2-NΔ47 variants expressed at 42% and 23% that of the full-length protein, respectively (
Fig. 2
B
). Removal of 28 amino acids upstream of the canonical sequences of the bovine protein (ATP8A2-NΔ28) also reduced expression to 42% of the longer bovine ATP8A2 protein (
Fig. 2
C
). These studies do not directly determine whether the most N-terminal 12 (human) or 9 (bovine) amino acids contribute to the expression of the protein, but it is reasonable to speculate that any effect of these residues would be minor.

To further assess the effect of these substitutions on protein stability, we used FoldX5, a well-established force field and modeling program (

Discussion
In this study, we have examined the structural features of the N- and C-terminal segments of ATP8A2 and assessed their role in protein expression, subcellular localization, and activity. In the case of the N-terminal segment, there has been considerable uncertainty regarding the initiation site of ATP8A2 and accordingly, the length of this segment and the size of the flippase. Mouse ATP8A2 (
P98200
) appears to use the AUG at the beginning of the canonical region as its methionine start codon since the upstream sequence of its RNA transcript is devoid of in-frame AUG codons and contains an in-frame stop codon (
Figs. 1
A
and
S2
). Human and bovine ATP8A2 transcripts, however, have two upstream methionine codons either of which can potentially serve as an initiation site, and this region is devoid of an in-frame stop codon (
Figs. 1
A
,
S1
and
S2
). The methionine residue 40 amino acids upstream of the canonical methionine in human ATP8A2 has been generally considered as the start site resulting in a full-length protein of 1188 amino acids (
Q9NTI2
). The initiation site of bovine ATP8A2 is of interest since it has been widely used in structure–function studies (
21
). Initially, the methionine residue 28 amino acids upstream of the canonical sequence of bovine ATP8A2 was considered as the start site yielding a protein of 1176 amino acids (
36
). However, more recently, bovine ATP8A2 (
C7EXK4
) has been listed in the UniProt database to contain 1148 amino acids with a methionine start site at the beginning of the canonical sequence to coincide with mouse ATP8A2. LC–MS/MS of ATP8A2 from bovine retina, however, clearly show the presence of numerous unique tryptic peptides upstream of the canonical sequence (
Fig. 1
D
and
Table 1
). This indicates that the primary ATP8A2 initiation site is the methionine residue 37 residues upstream of the canonical start site methionine yielding a protein of 1185 amino acids, a finding in general agreement with the human ortholog. It is possible that there are alternative start sites in other tissues (
51
,
52
), but this remains to be determined. We have scanned the ATP8A2 database for a wide variety of other mammalian species (
Fig. S1
). With the exception of the mouse ortholog, all these ATP8A2 proteins appear to have an extended N-terminal sequence that has considerable sequence conservation. The AlphaFold-2-derived structure of human ATP8A2 predicts the KKAEDEMSRA sequence within the N terminus to have an α-helical secondary structure, but the model does not reveal the existence of interactions of this or other N-terminal segments with other domains of ATP8A2.
Heterologous expression studies indicate that the extended N-terminal segment increases the expression of functionally active human and bovine ATP8A2. The N-terminal segment may stabilize the protein through either transient interactions with other domains of ATP8A2 or the binding to a chaperone protein during the folding process. Although the N-terminal segment enhances protein expression, it does not appear to significantly affect the subcellular localization or alter the functional properties of ATP8A2. This is further supported by the finding that mouse ATP8A2 lacking the upstream N-terminal sequence, nevertheless, plays a critical functional role in neuronal cell development and sensory physiology (
37
,
42
). We conclude that the N-terminal segment of ATP8A2 does not play a major role in the regulation or function of this phospholipid flippase, but it does enhance the expression level of the protein at least in heterologous cell expression systems. It is not known why mouse AT8A2 lacks the extended N-terminal segment present in human and bovine ATP8A2 and for that matter other mammalian ATP8A2 proteins. However, it is of note that the start and length of translated exon 1 is quite different in the mouse gene (
Fig. S2
). This divergence in mouse
ATP8A2
gene remains a topic for further investigation.
The C-terminal segment has been shown to regulate the functional activity of a number of P4-ATPases through an autoinhibition mechanism. A significant increase in the phospholipid-induced ATPase activity was observed when the C-terminal tail of ATP8B1 or Drs2 was removed (
30
,
31
,
32
). Structural studies show that this segment including the “GYAFS” motif (AYAFS in ATP8B1 and GFAFS in Drs2) interacts with the cytoplasmic catalytic domains (
25
,
28
,
30
). C-terminal deletion mutations have also pointed to a role of the C-terminal tail in the folding and regulation of ATP8A2 (
47
). To more clearly define the role of the C-terminal tail in the protein expression and functional activity, we expressed full-length ATP8A2 containing a TEV cleavage site upstream of the GYAFS motif (
Fig. 6
A
). This enabled us to remove the C-terminal tail by TEV proteolysis after the purification of the protein for analysis of PS-activated ATPase activity. The observed increase in specific PS-dependent ATPase activity and decrease in
K
m
for ATP is consistent with a role of the C terminus in autoinhibition. The structure of ATP8A2 has not been reported. However, the structure of ATP8A1, which shares a high degree of sequence conservation (67% sequence identity) and phospholipid-dependent ATPase activity with ATP8A2, has been determined in various states by cryo-EM (
23
). In its E2P state, the GYAFS motif is seen to interact with the ATP binding site within the N domain. This interaction between the GFAFS motif and the ATP binding site is also observed in yeast Drs2 (
27
,
28
).
Downstream serine residues (S1131 and S1133) also appear to form polar contacts with a glutamate residue (E533) in the N domain of ATP8A1 (
Fig. S4
). Similar interactions of the GYAFS and a downstream serine (S1170) are predicted in the AlphaFold-2 model of human ATP8A2. Collectively, these studies are consistent with the C-terminal tail being involved in modest autoinhibition of ATP8A2 and support the previous suggestion that a C-terminal autoinhibition mechanism may be a feature common to many P4-ATPases (
30
).
To specifically define the role of the C-terminal GYAFS motif in the stability and function of human ATP8A2, we individually replaced each residue with alanine or a related amino acid. Replacement of the glycine, tyrosine, and phenylalanine with alanine resulted in a severe reduction in the expression of ATP8A2 without affecting their catalytic activity. Destabilization of these variants was also predicted using the FoldX-5 stability software. This prediction assumes that these mutations do not affect mRNA expression or translation efficiency. This is supported by previous studies in which destabilizing disease variants did not have an effect on mRNA levels in the over cell expression system (
44
). When the tyrosine and phenylalanine residues within this motif were substituted for a different aromatic residue, we observed significant expression levels indicating that aromaticity is essential at these positions by providing π–π interactions with the F569 in the N domain. These studies support the view that the GYAFS through its interaction with the ATP binding site plays a crucial role in the folding of ATP8A2 consistent with earlier studies invoking a role of the C-terminal tail in the proper folding of ATP8A2 into a functional transporter (
47
).
In summary, we show experimentally that bovine, like human, ATP8A2 contains an extended N-terminal sequence not apparent in the mouse ortholog that enhances the expression of ATP8A2 without affecting its subcellular localization or PS-activated ATPase activity. The C-terminal segment of ATP8A2, like ATP8B1 and ATP8A1, most likely interacts with the catalytic domains resulting in a modest autoinhibition of activity. While this phenomenon appears modest, it may be that this is one of several mechanisms involved in regulating the activity of this flippase. The C-terminal segment is further involved in stabilizing the protein during the folding process.
Experimental procedures
Reagents
1,2-Dioleoyl-
sn
-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC) and 1,2-dioleoyl-
sn
-glycero-3-phospho-L-serine (DOPS) were purchased from Avanti Polar Lipids, Inc. ATP and ascorbic acid were purchased from Sigma–Aldrich, CHAPS from Anatrace, ProteaseArrest inhibitor cocktail from G-Biosciences, and 1D4 peptide from Biomatik. HEK293T and HeLa cells were purchased from American Type Culture Collection through Cedarlane Laboratories. The Rho 1D4 antibody used in the immunoaffinity columns was initially generated in-house (
53
); the purified antibody was obtained from the University of British Columbia (
https://uilo.ubc.ca/industry-partners/access-ubc-technologies
). Primary antibodies against tubulin were ordered from Abcam (ab15568). Primary antibodies against ATP8A2 (ATP6C11) used in Western blots were raised in-house (
19
,
36
). Restriction enzymes, T4-DNA ligase, Antarctic Phosphatase, and Phusion polymerase were acquired from New England Biolabs. Primers used for mutagenesis were ordered from Integrated DNA Technologies. Purified TEV protease was received as a gift by Dr Van Petegem (UBC).
N- and C-terminal mutant construct design
The bovine and human ATP8A2 constructs containing a C-terminal 1D4 tag were previously developed in a pcDNA3.1 plasmid (
36
). The single amino acid substitutions in the GYAFS motif were generated by designing specific overlapping primers with mismatched nucleotides for PCR using Phusion polymerase. A construct containing a TEV protease cut site (ENLYFQ▼S) inserted at the −60 C-terminal amino acid position was created using overlapping primer design. Constructs were created in which the start codons of the human ATP8A2 construct were truncated to the 40th and 47th amino acid position. These constructs were then ligated back into the WT plasmid construct using the KpnI and EcoRI restriction enzymes. The bovine ATP8A2 N terminus was truncated at the 37th amino acid using PCR and ligated back into the original plasmid construct using the KpnI and BamHI restriction enzymes.
Cell culture and protein expression
HEK293T cells were cultured using DMEM (Sigma–Aldrich) supplemented with 8% bovine growth serum (Thermo Scientific), 100 IU/ml penicillin, 100 μg/ml streptomycin, and 2 mM
l
-glutamine. The cells were grown to ∼30% confluency in 10 cm plates at which point they were cotransfected with 5 μg of the ATP8A2 construct and 5 μg CDC50A plasmid and 30 μg of polyethylenimine as a transfection reagent. The cells were harvested after 48 h and pelleted at 2000 rcf (Sorvall LegendRT). The cells were resuspended in lysis buffer (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM Hepes/NaOH [pH 7.5], 5 mM MgCl
2
, 20 mM CHAPS, 1× Protease Arrest, 1 mM DTT, and 0.5 mg/ml DOPC). The resuspended cells were lysed by stirring at 4 °C for 30 min. After lysis, the detergent insoluble membrane fraction was removed from the detergent soluble fraction by centrifugation at 40,000 rcf for 12 min. The solubilized ATP8A2–CDC50A proteins were then used for downstream applications. Protein expression was measured using Western blot analysis and normalized to a tubulin loading control (see later).
Immunoaffinity protein purification
Purification of the ATP8A2–CDC50a complex was achieved using immunoaffinity column chromatography as previously described (
19
,
36
). Immunoaffinity columns were prepared through the coupling of the Rho1D4 or ATP6C11 monoclonal antibodies to CNBr-activated Sepharose 2B beads as described previously (
36
,
54
). Typically, the detergent-solubilized cell lysate was incubated with the immunoaffinity matrix for 45 min at 4 °C. The unbound protein was then removed by centrifugation, and the spin column containing the immunoaffinity matrix was then washed six times with 400 μl of column wash buffer (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM Hepes/NaOH pH 7.5, 5 mM MgCl
2
, 10 mM CHAPS, 1 mM DTT, and 0.5 mg/ml DOPC). The bound protein was eluted from the column using 2 × 50 μl of wash buffer containing 0.5 mg/ml of the 6C11 or 1D4 peptide. Purified protein concentration was determined from SDS-PAGE stained with Coomassie blue and quantified relative to bovine serum albumin as standards.
TEV cleavage of TEV-modified ATP8A2
The ATP8A2 construct containing a C-terminal TEV cut site was purified as described. After purification and quantification, the sample was incubated with TEV protease at a ∼1:1 w/w ratio at 4 °C overnight. Uncleaved ATP8A2 and C-terminal peptide fragments were removed by binding to an anti-6C11 immunoaffinity column. This was verified using Western blot analysis in combination with Coomassie-stained SDS gels.
ATPase assays
The ATPase activity of the purified ATP8A2 constructs was assayed using a previously described colorimetric method (
36
,
55
). To measure the ATPase activity as a function of lipid substrate, 1 ng of purified protein was incubated with 5 mM ATP and 2.5 mg/ml of different ratios of DOPC:DOPS. To measure the velocity as a function of ATP concentration, 1 ng of protein was incubated with 2.5 mg/ml of lipid mixture (68:32 DOPC:DOPS), and variable concentrations of ATP ranging from 0 mM to 5 mM. The ATP and lipid samples were prepared in ATPase assay buffer (50 mM Hepes/NaOH, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 12.5 mM MgCl
2
, 1 mM DTT, and 10 mM CHAPS). This mixture was prepared up to 25 μl and was incubated at 37 °C for 30 min. The activity of the protein was terminated through the addition of 25 μl of 12% SDS. The free phosphate was measured by the addition of 75 μl of solution 1 (6% ascorbic acid and 1% ammonium molybdate in 1 N HCl) for 5 min, followed by 120 μl of solution II (2% sodium citrate, 2% sodium meta-arsenite, and 2% acetic acid). The reaction of solution 1 and solution 2 results in a color shift allowing for the measurement of free phosphate absorbance at 850 nm in a microplate reader. These values were compared to those of a phosphate standard curve allowing for calculation of the reaction velocity (micromoles of Pi released/minute/milligram protein) for each data point in the given assay. Each measurement was performed in technical triplicates. Michaelis–Menten equation was used to fit the data and obtain maximum reaction velocity (
V
max
), PS-activation constant (
K
a
), and PS-activation constant (
K
a
) and
K
m
for ATP.
Immunofluorescence microscopy
HeLa cells grown on glass coverslips in six-well tissue culture plates were cotransfected at 50% confluence with 1.25 μg of ATP8A2-1D4 and 1.25 μg of CDC50A plasmids using polyethylenimine as a transfection agent. After 48 h, the cells were washed in PBS and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, then blocked and permeabilized for 1 h with 10% normal goat serum (Sigma–Aldrich, NS02L) and 0.2% Triton X-100. The cells were treated for 2 h with primary antibody diluted in 100 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) containing 2.5% normal goat serum and 0.05% Triton X-100. The primary antibodies were Rho1D4 hybridoma culture fluid (1:50 dilution), and rabbit anti-GM130 antibody (1:2000, SAB5700801; Sigma–Aldrich) for labeling the cis-Golgi. The coverslips were washed and labeled with goat antimouse immunoglobulin tagged with AlexaFluor 488 (A11029; Thermo Fisher Scientific) and goat antirabbit immunoglobulin tagged with AlexaFluor 594 (A11012; Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 0.5 h and stained with the nuclear dye 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole. Coverslips were washed and mounted with Mowiol medium (Sigma–Aldrich; 32459-0) on glass slides prior to imaging. The reagents for fixing, permeabilizing, and labeling were prepared in 100 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.4). The secondary antibodies were used at 1:1000 dilution. Fluorescence images were acquired using a 63× oil immersion objective on a Zeiss LSM 700 confocal microscope equipped with Zen Image analysis software (
https://www.zeiss.com/microscopy/en/products/software/zeiss-zen-lite.html
). Composite figures were prepared using Photoshop software. Quantification of colocalization was performed using Coloc2, a plugin of ImageJ (National Institutes of Health,
https://imagej.nih.gov/ij/
). The Pearson correlation coefficient was reported for the ATP8A2 and GM130 signals.
SDS-PAGE and Western blotting
Proteins were separated by SDS gel electrophoresis on 9% polyacrylamide gels and either stained with Coomassie blue or transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride membranes (Millipore) and blocked with 1% milk in PBS for 45 min as previously described (
44
). The blots were labeled with hybridoma cell culture fluid containing the Rho1D4 antibody (diluted 1:100 in PBS). The blots were also labeled with antitubulin antibody (1:3000 dilution) serving as a loading control. After 1 h, the gels were washed stringently with PBS containing 0.05% Tween-20 (PBST), incubated for 40 min with secondary antibody (goat antimouse conjugated with IR dye 680 or donkey antirabbit conjugated with IR dye 800; 926-68070 and 926-32213; LI-COR) diluted 1:20,000 in PBST containing 0.5% milk. After washing in PBST, the blots were imaged on a LI-COR Odyssey infrared imaging system (
https://www.licor.com/bio/image-studio-lite/
).

in silico
stability predictions
The stability of WT and ATP8A2 clones was predicted using FoldX5 (
https://foldxsuite.crg.eu/
) (
50
) as previously described (
43
). The protein structures were generated in AlphaFold2 (
56
) and repaired using the FoldX5 plugin with the YASARA viewer (
http://www.yasara.org/
). The structure of ATP8A2 (accession number:
Q9NTI2
) was accessed from the AlphaFold database (
https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/
). This was accessed on July 10, 2023. The Gibbs free energy change was calculated and reported as ΔΔGmutant−ΔΔGWT. PyMOL Molecular Graphics System (version 1.7; Schrodinger) was used to display structures.
LC–MS/MS analysis
Protein samples for MS analysis were purified from bovine rod outer segments and HEK293T transfected cells using immunoaffinity protein purification. Rod outer segments were isolated from bovine retina as previously described (
57
) and solubilized in 20 mM CHAPS detergent. The cell lysate was incubated with Atp-6C11 antibody conjugated to Sepharose 4B. The beads were eluted using 50 μl of SDS elution buffer (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM Hepes/NaOH [pH 7.5], 5 mM MgCl
2
, 1% SDS, 1 mM DTT, and 0.5 mg/ml DOPC). Approximately 5 μg of purified protein sample was acquired for each condition. The samples were then subjected to proteolysis for MS using the filter-aided sample preparation as described previously (
15
,
58
).
Samples were reconstituted in 0.5% acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid. Sample concentration was measured using NanoDrop One (Thermo Scientific) with the A205 Scope method (absorbance at 205 nm, baseline correction at 340 nm). About 100 ng of peptides were injected and separated on-line using NanoElute 2 UHPLC system (Bruker Daltonics) with Aurora Series Gen3 (CSI) analytical column, (25 cm × 75 μm 1.7 μm C18 120 Å, with CSI fitting; Ion Opticks). The analytical column was heated to 50 °C using a column toaster M (Bruker Daltonics). The NanoElute thermostat temperature was set at 7 °C. Buffer A consisted of 0.1% aqueous formic acid and 0.5% acetonitrile in water, and buffer B consisted of 0.1% aqueous formic acid and 0.5% water in acetonitrile. Before each run, the analytical column was conditioned with four column volumes of buffer A. The analysis was performed at 0.30 μl/min flow rate. A standard 30 min gradient was run from 2% B to 12% B over 15 min, then to 33% B from 15 to 30 min, then to 95% B over 0.5 min, held at 95% B for 7.72 min. Liquid chromatography was coupled to a Trapped Ion Mobility-Time of Flight mass spectrometer with dual TIMS (TimsTOF Pro2; Bruker Daltonics). The captive spray ionization source was operated at 1800 V capillary voltage, 3 L/min drying gas, and 180 °C drying temperature. During analysis, the TimsTOF Pro 2 was operated with parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation scan mode for data-dependent acquisition. The MS and MS/MS spectra were collected in positive mode, from
m/z
100 Th to

TIMS-MS scan was set at equal ramp time and accumulation time of 100 ms, at a rate of 9.42 Hz (100% duty cycle). Active exclusion was enabled with a 0.4 min release and reconsidered if their intensity increased more than four times. For each TIMS cycle, five parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation MS/MS scans were recorded (total cycle time = 0.64 s).
